concepts.name: Lorenz Curve: Construction and Geometric Interpretation
key_dimensions: How cumulative population share (x-axis) maps against cumulative income/wealth share (y-axis)
The role of the 45-degree line of perfect equality as a reference benchmark
Why the Lorenz curve always lies below or on the line of perfect equality (convexity property)
Distinction between Lorenz curves for income vs. wealth distributions and what a crossing Lorenz curve implies

concepts.name: Gini Coefficient: Mathematical Definition and Derivation from Lorenz Curve
key_dimensions: Gini = Area A / (Area A + Area B), where A is the gap between perfect equality line and Lorenz curve
Range of Gini coefficient: 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality) — why it cannot exceed 1
Alternative formula: Gini as half the relative mean absolute difference between all pairs of incomes
UPSC trap: Gini of 0 does not mean zero poverty; it means equal distribution at any income level

concepts.name: Perfect Equality vs. Perfect Inequality: Extreme Cases on the Lorenz Curve
key_dimensions: Perfect equality: Lorenz curve coincides with the 45-degree diagonal; Gini = 0
Perfect inequality: Lorenz curve runs along both axes (one person owns everything); Gini = 1
Why pure perfect inequality is a theoretical construct never observed in practice
Policy implication: Any real economy's Lorenz curve lies strictly between these two extremes

concepts.name: Gini Coefficient as a Measure of Relative vs. Absolute Inequality
key_dimensions: Gini captures relative inequality (shares), not absolute income gaps — critical distinction
Two countries with same Gini can have vastly different absolute poverty levels (UPSC trap)
Why economic growth can reduce absolute poverty while Gini remains unchanged or worsens
Comparison with absolute inequality measures like the Theil Index and Atkinson Index

concepts.name: Limitations and Criticisms of the Gini Coefficient
key_dimensions: Insensitivity to where inequality occurs: same Gini can result from inequality at top vs. bottom of distribution
Cannot capture multidimensional inequality (health, education, gender) — contrast with MPI
Crossing Lorenz curves problem: two distributions with crossing curves can yield identical Gini values
Does not account for negative incomes, making it less reliable for wealth inequality measurement

concepts.name: Crossing Lorenz Curves and Ambiguity in Inequality Comparison
key_dimensions: When two Lorenz curves intersect, neither distribution unambiguously dominates the other
Lorenz dominance: Distribution A is unambiguously more equal than B only if A's curve never crosses B's
Implication: Gini alone cannot rank societies when curves cross — need supplementary measures
UPSC angle: This is why a single statistic like Gini is insufficient for comprehensive policy analysis

concepts.name: India's Gini Coefficient: Trends and Contextual Data
key_dimensions: India's income Gini (approx. 0.35–0.38) vs. wealth Gini (approx. 0.65–0.74) — stark divergence
Oxfam and World Inequality Report findings: top 1% holding disproportionate wealth share in India
Rural vs. urban Gini differences and the role of land ownership in wealth concentration
Post-liberalisation trend: India's Gini has risen, suggesting growth has not been uniformly inclusive

concepts.name: Global Gini Comparisons and India's Position
key_dimensions: High-inequality countries: South Africa (~0.63), Brazil (~0.53); low-inequality: Nordic countries (~0.25–0.29)
India vs. China Gini comparison — China's Gini rose sharply with rapid growth (Kuznets curve link)
Between-country vs. within-country Gini: global inequality measured by combining both components
UPSC trap: A lower Gini than a peer nation does not imply lower poverty — purchasing power and base income matter

concepts.name: Kuznets Inverted-U Hypothesis and Its Relationship with the Gini Coefficient
key_dimensions: Kuznets curve: inequality (Gini) first rises then falls as per-capita income increases during development
Stages: agrarian economy → industrialisation (Gini rises) → mature economy (Gini falls)
Empirical criticism: Many developing nations show rising Gini even at advanced stages — hypothesis challenged
India's trajectory as a test case: IT/services-led growth vs. manufacturing-led growth and inequality outcomes

concepts.name: Wealth Gini vs. Income Gini: Why Wealth Inequality Is Always Higher
key_dimensions: Wealth accumulates over generations (inheritance); income is a flow variable — structural difference
Negative incomes are possible but negative wealth is bounded, affecting Gini calculation differently
India's wealth Gini (~0.74) far exceeds income Gini (~0.35) — policy implication for wealth/inheritance tax debate
Piketty's r > g argument: return on capital exceeding growth rate perpetually widens wealth Gini

concepts.name: Lorenz Curve Applications Beyond Income: Consumption, Land, and Health Inequality
key_dimensions: Consumption Lorenz curve used in India's NSSO/PLFS data — preferred over income data due to reliability
Land distribution Lorenz curve: highlights agrarian inequality relevant to land reform debates
Health inequality: Concentration curves (extension of Lorenz) measure inequality in health outcomes
UPSC angle: Economic Survey uses consumption-based Gini, not income-based — understanding data source matters

concepts.name: Gini Coefficient and the Palma Ratio: Complementary Inequality Metrics
key_dimensions: Palma Ratio = income share of top 10% / income share of bottom 40% — more policy-intuitive than Gini
Palma addresses Gini's weakness of over-sensitivity to middle of distribution; focuses on extremes
UN and UNDP increasingly recommend Palma alongside Gini for SDG monitoring (SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities)
India's Palma ratio context: highlights how the top decile's share dwarfs gains for the bottom two quintiles

concepts.name: Gini Coefficient and Poverty: Why They Measure Different Phenomena
key_dimensions: Poverty is an absolute threshold concept; Gini is a relative distributional concept — fundamentally different
A country can have low Gini but high poverty (equal misery) or high Gini with low poverty (unequal prosperity)
UPSC trap: Reduction in Gini does not necessarily mean reduction in poverty headcount ratio
Need to read Gini alongside poverty lines (Tendulkar, Rangarajan) and MPI for comprehensive assessment

concepts.name: Decomposition of the Gini Coefficient: Within-Group and Between-Group Inequality
key_dimensions: Total inequality = Within-group inequality + Between-group inequality + Overlap/interaction term
Application: decomposing India's Gini into rural-urban, caste, gender, or sectoral components
Policy use: if between-group inequality dominates, targeted group-specific policies are more effective
Limitation: Gini is not perfectly decomposable (unlike Theil Index), creating an overlap residual term

concepts.name: Lorenz Curve and Social Welfare Functions: Normative Dimensions
key_dimensions: Atkinson's theorem: if one Lorenz curve dominates another, all inequality-averse social welfare functions prefer it
Link between Lorenz dominance and Pareto efficiency — Pareto improvement does not guarantee Lorenz improvement
Rawlsian maximin principle vs. utilitarian principle: different ethical positions imply different preferred Lorenz positions
UPSC angle: distributive justice debates (Rawls, Sen's capability approach) have direct measurable counterparts in Lorenz analysis

concepts.name: NSSO/PLFS Data and Measurement of Consumption Inequality in India
key_dimensions: MPCE (Monthly Per Capita Expenditure) from HCES used to plot Lorenz curve and derive consumption Gini
Controversy: 2017–18 NSSO data reportedly suppressed due to showing rising consumption inequality
HCES 2022–23 revival: new data providing updated picture of consumption distribution post-COVID
UPSC trap: India lacks a comprehensive, regular income survey — consumption Gini is a proxy with its own biases (underreporting of top incomes)

concepts.name: Policy Interventions Aimed at Shifting the Lorenz Curve Towards Equality
key_dimensions: Progressive taxation: steeper income/wealth tax shifts after-tax Lorenz curve closer to equality line
Direct benefit transfers (DBT), MGNREGA, PM-KISAN: targeted at bottom quintiles to lift the left portion of the curve
Public expenditure on education and health: reduces opportunity inequality, affecting long-run Lorenz position
UPSC angle: evaluate whether India's fiscal policy is effectively compressing the Lorenz curve — pre-tax vs. post-tax Gini comparison

concepts.name: Gini Coefficient in the Context of SDG 10 and India's Voluntary National Review
key_dimensions: SDG Target 10.1: achieve income growth of bottom 40% at rate higher than national average (Palma/Lorenz logic embedded)
India's Voluntary National Review (VNR) submissions and reporting on inequality indicators
Tension between India's GDP growth narrative and persisting high wealth concentration (Oxfam reports)
UPSC angle: how international commitments under SDGs create accountability for Gini/inequality trends in domestic policymaking

concepts.name: Thomas Piketty's Wealth Inequality Framework and Its Gini Implications for India
key_dimensions: r > g thesis: when return on capital (r) exceeds economic growth rate (g), wealth Gini structurally worsens
World Inequality Database (WID) data on India: top 1% income share rising — corroborated by rising wealth Gini
Policy prescription: progressive wealth tax, inheritance tax as tools to compress wealth Lorenz curve
UPSC angle: Piketty's framework used to critique liberalisation-era policies — contrast with trickle-down growth arguments

concepts.name: Gender Dimension of the Gini Coefficient and Lorenz Curve
key_dimensions: Standard Gini calculated on household income may mask intra-household gender inequality
Gender Wage Gap as a component contributing to overall income Gini — women's lower labour force participation in India
Feminist economics critique: Lorenz curve ignores unpaid care work, understating women's economic contribution
UPSC angle: Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Inequality Index (GII) complement Gini in capturing gendered distributional outcomes
